requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory on node1
requirements.summary: Directory created with mkdir/chmod 1777; stat confirms mode 1777, drwxrwxrwt, owner=root group=root, directly observed both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop (sticky bit enforcement)
requirements.summary: Live test with dropuser1/dropuser2 shows dropuser2's rm of dropuser1's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' while dropuser2 could write its own file and dropuser1 could delete its own file, confirming both the writable and no-cross-delete properties. Re-verified after restart with fresh users (verifyuser1/verifyuser2) showing identical behavior.

requirements.requirement: Directory remains shared/writable to all users (any user can write, per 'shared writable directory')
requirements.summary: Both dropuser1 and dropuser2 successfully wrote their own files into /srv/drop, confirming world-writability alongside the sticky-bit restriction.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (pre-restart boot identity/health, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity, recovered service/data/config state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 33b0e84c... and /srv/drop state; backgrounded 'shutdown -r now' returned an immediate ack; a subsequent connection attempt timed out confirming the node was down; reconnection showed a new boot_id 3934e984... and new uptime; /srv/drop permissions/ownership and sticky-bit behavior were re-verified post-restart with fresh test users. This is corroborated by the fixed after_prepare (33b0e84c...) and after_executor (3934e984...) boot-identity snapshots, which match the executor's own before/after values.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /srv/drop as a world-writable directory (mode 1777, root:root) and directly demonstrated, via live multi-user tests both before and after a full reboot, that non-owning users cannot delete each other's files while owners and any user can still write. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a coherent pre-restart baseline, acknowledged reboot, connection-loss confirmation, changed boot identity, and post-restart re-verification of both directory configuration and sticky-bit behavior, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Operational hygiene is good: all test users/files were cleaned up and the sole leftover artifact is a small /tmp/reboot.log from the required reboot command.
limitations: Native package-manager consistency check was unavailable (timed out) both before and after the executor's work, so package-state integrity around the restart cannot be independently confirmed from evidence; this appears to be a pre-existing platform limitation rather than something caused by the executor.
/tmp/reboot.log residue left after the restart was not explicitly assessed for content sensitivity, though it is a low-risk shutdown log.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to the task: directory creation (cmd-64c0dcb1c27b40ea), bounded test-user creation/deletion used to prove sticky-bit behavior both pre- and post-restart (cmd-c95ab2b643654968, cmd-3b8f55bcfdaf42bb, cmd-6ed005d47fb44950, cmd-7dd6751809424008), and the mandated restart cycle (cmd-bc631d31341d4103). All test users and test files were fully removed (cmd-b45d5209a1004df0, and cleanup within cmd-7dd6751809424008), leaving /srv/drop empty and correctly permissioned. The first command (cmd-7431aafa37c14003) failed with 'Permission denied' due to missing sudo and caused no state change; it was immediately corrected. One minor residue was introduced by the reboot command itself: /tmp/reboot.log (redirect target of the backgrounded 'shutdown -r now') is present in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was not cleaned up; this is low-risk, expected exhaust from a required action and not deliberately retained state, but it is uncleaned residue.
